title: The Real Cost of Stock Photography
summary: Stock photography pricing ranges from $2.50 to $499 for a single image. Here is what drives the gap, how licenses work, and when a real shoot is cheaper.
body_markdown:
## The same picture, two very different invoices


*The archetypal stock frame. What you pay depends on how you buy it, not what it shows.*


Two buyers download a photo of a woman in an office on the same afternoon. One pays $2.50. One pays $499. Same category of image, same resolution, wildly different invoice.


That gap confuses people because they assume they are buying a photograph. They are not. They are buying a licence, and the price tracks commitment, exclusivity, and permitted use rather than the picture itself. Once you can read the pricing that way, choosing between platforms takes about five minutes.


Here is what the major libraries actually charge in 2026, what moves the number, and the point at which commissioning your own photographs becomes the cheaper option.


## What the big three actually charge


Shutterstock is the volume play. Its 10-image monthly subscription is $25 a month, billed yearly at $300, which works out at $2.50 an image. Unlimited image downloads run $29 a month billed yearly at $348, and a broader Unlimited Plus plan covering images, video, music, and AI generations is $69 a month, $828 a year. Buying without a subscription is far worse value: a two-image pack is $29, or $14.50 each.


Getty Images sits at the other end deliberately. Its creative image subscription is $225 a month on an annual plan for 10 downloads, or $22.49 per image, with an editorial-only tier at $167 a month, $16.66 per image. Buy a single creative image outright and the standard price is $499. Its commitment-free UltraPack starts at $1,800 for five downloads, $360 each.


Adobe Stock lands between them, and is worth it mainly if your team lives inside Creative Cloud. Adobe's own plan documentation references US$29.99, US$79.99, and US$99.99 monthly tiers with credit rollover.


So the cheapest subscription image and the most expensive single licence sit orders of magnitude apart. The photography does not.


## The four things you are actually paying for


*A university mark and a real person. That is what the indemnity line on a licence covers.*


Commitment. Annual subscriptions are the cheapest per image by a wide margin, and one-off packs are the most expensive. If you buy stock more than twice a year, a subscription is almost always correct.


Exclusivity. Getty's premium tiers exist because a large share of that library is not available elsewhere. Shutterstock's contributor pool overlaps heavily with other platforms, which is exactly why your competitor's landing page has your hero image on it.


License type. A standard royalty-free licence covers most web, social, and marketing use. Extended or enhanced licenses are needed for merchandise, templates for resale, and unlimited print runs, and they cost more. Rights-managed licences, priced per use and territory, are a different model again.


Indemnification. Enterprise licensing bundles legal cover, and both Getty and Adobe publish coverage of up to $10,000 per file on standard plans. For a regulated industry that line item is the whole reason to pay more.


## When a real shoot becomes the cheaper option


*Faces turned away, nobody in particular. Exactly the frame eye-tracking says readers skip.*


Run the arithmetic honestly and stock stops winning sooner than people expect.


Twenty Getty creative images at the $22.49 subscription rate is $450. Five images from an UltraPack is $1,800. A Snappr shoot with a vetted local photographer starts at under $100 and returns edited, exclusive images of your actual product, premises, or team within 48 hours. At Getty prices, a single afternoon's shoot is cost-competitive with a handful of licenses, and you own the results outright.


The performance gap makes the maths worse for stock. Nielsen Norman Group's eye-tracking found that users scrutinise photos of real people and products and ignore stock photos of generic models almost entirely. A cheap image nobody looks at has a worse cost per impression than an expensive one they study.


We have catalogued[the stock photos everyone has already seen too many times](https://www.snappr.com/blog/10-most-overused-stock-photos) , and written up the case for[replacing stock with real images](https://www.snappr.com/blog/how-replacing-stock-photos-with-professional-images-can-increase-leads-by-45) . The short version: use stock for backgrounds, textures, and concepts. Shoot anything a customer will judge you on.


## The honest split


Most teams should do both. Licence stock for the things nobody scrutinises: abstract backgrounds, illustrative spot images, filler for internal decks. Commission photography for products, premises, people, and anything appearing on a page where someone decides whether to buy.


That split usually costs less overall than either extreme, because it stops you paying Getty rates for a background texture and stops you shipping a stock handshake on your homepage.


[Book a shoot with Snappr](https://www.snappr.com/shoots) for the images your customers will actually look at, and keep the subscription for everything else.


## Frequently asked questions


### How much does stock photography cost?


Between $2.50 and $499 per image in 2026, depending on the platform and how you buy. Shutterstock's 10-image annual subscription works out at the low end, while a single standard Getty Images creative licence sits at the high end.


### Is a stock photo subscription cheaper than buying images individually?


Almost always, and by a large margin. A Shutterstock two-image pack is $29, while the same two images on the annual 10-download plan cost about $5 in total. Subscriptions only lose if you genuinely need fewer than a handful of images a year.


### What is the difference between royalty-free and rights-managed?


A royalty-free licence is paid once and permits broad ongoing use within the terms, with no per-use fee. A rights-managed licence is priced for a specific use, territory, duration, and print run, and can include exclusivity. Royalty-free suits most marketing work.


### Do I need an extended license?


Only if the image will appear on products for resale, in templates or merchandise, or in print runs beyond the standard licence cap. Normal website, social, advertising, and presentation use is covered by a standard licence on all major platforms.


### When is commissioning photography cheaper than buying stock?


Once you need more than a handful of premium images, or any image of your own product, premises, or team. A short professional shoot starts at[under $100](https://www.snappr.com/shoots) and delivers exclusive images, while five Getty UltraPack downloads cost $1,800.
